title: Book V: The Dead Hand — Chapter L
paragraphs:
“This Loller here wol precilen us somewhat.”
“Nay by my father’s soule! that schal he nat,”
Sayde the Schipman, ‘here schal he not preche,
We schal no gospel glosen here ne teche.
We leven all in the gret God,’ quod he.
He wolden sowen some diffcultee.”—_Canterbury Tales_.

Dorothea had been safely installed at Freshitt Hall for nearly a week before she asked any dangerous questions. Each morning she now sat with Celia in the prettiest of the upstairs sitting rooms, which opened into a small conservatory. Dressed in white and lavender, like a bunch of mixed violets, Celia watched her baby’s remarkable activities. To her inexperienced mind they were so mysterious that she kept interrupting every conversation to ask the all-knowing nurse to interpret them. Beside her sat Dorothea in mourning, looking far too sad for Celia’s liking. After all, the baby was perfectly well; and really, when a husband had been so tedious and troublesome alive, and had besides—well, well! Sir James had, of course, told Celia everything, impressing on her how important it was to keep Dorothea ignorant until telling her became unavoidable.

But Mr. Brooke had correctly predicted that Dorothea would not remain inactive for long when responsibilities had been given to her. She knew the substance of the will her husband had made at their marriage. As soon as she clearly understood her situation, she began quietly considering her duties as owner of Lowick Manor, including her right to appoint the parish clergyman.
One morning her uncle came for his customary visit, though in unusually lively spirits. He explained that it was now almost certain Parliament would be dissolved immediately. Dorothea said—

“Uncle, I ought now to consider who should have the living at Lowick. Once Mr. Tucker had been provided for, I never heard my husband mention any clergyman he had in mind to succeed him. I think I should have the keys now and go to Lowick to examine his papers. Something there may help me understand his wishes.”

“There’s no hurry, my dear,” Mr. Brooke said calmly. “You can go later, if you wish. But I looked through the desks and drawers—there was nothing—nothing except learned subjects, you know—and the will. Everything can wait. As for the living, I’ve already been asked to use my influence—a rather good candidate, I should say. Mr. Tyke has been recommended to me very strongly. I helped obtain an appointment for him before. An apostolic man, I believe—the sort of person who would suit you, my dear.”

“I’d like to know more about him, uncle, and decide for myself, if Mr. Casaubon has left no indication of his wishes. Perhaps he added something to the will—there may be instructions for me,” said Dorothea. Throughout their conversation she had been thinking of this possibility in connection with her husband’s work.
“Nothing about the rectory, my dear—nothing,” said Mr. Brooke. Getting up to leave, he held out his hand to his nieces. “Nor about his research, you know. Nothing in the will.”
Dorothea’s lip began to tremble.
“Come, my dear, you mustn’t think about these things yet. Later on, you know.”
“I’m quite well again, uncle. I want to do something.”

“Well, well, we’ll see. But I must hurry off—there’s no end to my work just now. It’s a crisis—a political crisis, you know. And here’s Celia with her little man—you’re an aunt now, you know, and I’m a sort of grandfather,” said Mr. Brooke in a placid rush. He was eager to get away and tell Chettam it would not be his fault if Dorothea insisted on examining everything.
When her uncle had gone, Dorothea sank back into her chair and looked thoughtfully down at her folded hands.
“Look, Dodo! Look at him! Have you ever seen anything like it?” said Celia, in her contented, clipped way.
“What is it, Kitty?” Dorothea asked, raising her eyes rather absently.

“What? His upper lip, of course. Look how he’s pulling it down, as though he were going to make a face. Isn’t it wonderful! Perhaps he’s having his own little thoughts. I wish nurse were here. Do look.”
A large tear, which had been gathering for some time, rolled down Dorothea’s cheek as she raised her eyes and tried to smile.
“Don’t be sad, Dodo. Kiss the baby. What are you brooding about? I’m sure you did everything—even far too much. You ought to be happy now.”
“I wonder whether Sir James would drive me to Lowick. I want to search through everything—to see whether any words were left for me.”

“You mustn’t go until Mr. Lydgate gives permission, and he hasn’t yet. Here you are, nurse: take baby and walk up and down the gallery. Besides, Dodo, you’ve got a mistaken idea in your head as usual. I can see it, and it upsets me.”

“What have I got wrong, Kitty?” Dorothea asked meekly. She was now almost prepared to believe that Celia was wiser than herself, and wondered with real anxiety what her mistaken idea might be. Celia recognized her advantage and meant to use it. None of the others knew Dodo as well as she did, or understood how to manage her. Since her baby’s birth, Celia had gained a new confidence in her own sound judgment and calm wisdom. It seemed obvious that where there was a baby, matters were satisfactory, and that error in general was simply the absence of that central balancing force.

“I can see exactly what you’re thinking, Dodo,” Celia said. “You’re trying to discover whether there’s something unpleasant you ought to do now, simply because Mr. Casaubon wanted it. As though you hadn’t been uncomfortable enough already. And he doesn’t deserve it, as you’ll find out. He’s behaved very badly. James is absolutely furious with him. I’d better tell you, to prepare you.”

“Celia,” Dorothea pleaded, “you’re distressing me. Please tell me at once what you mean.” The thought flashed through her mind that Mr. Casaubon had left his property to someone else—which would not be so very distressing.
“Well, he’s added a codicil to his will, saying you’d lose all the property if you married—I mean—”
“That doesn’t matter at all,” Dorothea interrupted impulsively.

“But if you married Mr. Ladislaw, not anyone else,” Celia continued with unshakable calm. “Of course, in one sense that doesn’t matter—you never _would_ marry Mr. Ladislaw. But that makes Mr. Casaubon’s behavior worse.”

Dorothea’s face and neck flushed painfully. Celia, however, believed she was administering a sobering dose of reality. It was filling her head with ideas that had damaged Dodo’s health so badly. So she continued in the same neutral voice, as if discussing the baby’s clothes.

“James says so. He says it’s abominable and quite unworthy of a gentleman. And nobody could judge better than James. It’s as though Mr. Casaubon wanted people to believe you’d wish to marry Mr. Ladislaw—which is ridiculous. Only James says it was meant to stop Mr. Ladislaw wanting to marry you for your money—as if he’d ever think of proposing to you. Mrs. Cadwallader said you might as well marry an Italian with white mice! But I must just see how baby’s doing,” Celia added in precisely the same tone. She threw a light shawl round her shoulders and tripped away.

By now Dorothea had gone cold again. She fell helplessly back in her chair. She might have described her experience as a vague, frightened awareness that her life was taking a new shape: she was undergoing a transformation in which memory could not adapt itself to the movement of newly formed organs. Everything looked different—her husband’s behavior, her sense of duty towards him, every conflict between them, and above all her entire relationship with Will Ladislaw. Her world was changing convulsively. The only clear thought she could form was that she must wait and think it all through again. One change frightened her as if it were a sin: a violent surge of revulsion from her dead husband, who had harbored secret thoughts, perhaps distorting everything she said and did. Then she felt another change, which also made her tremble—a sudden, unfamiliar longing for Will Ladislaw. It had never occurred to her that he might, under any circumstances, be her lover. Imagine the effect of suddenly learning that someone else had thought of him in that role—that perhaps he himself had recognized the possibility. And with that revelation came a rushing, jostling vision of unsuitable circumstances and questions that could not quickly be answered.

It seemed a long time—she could not tell how long—before she heard Celia saying, “That will do, nurse. He’ll sit quietly on my lap now. You can have your lunch, and leave Garratt in the next room. What I think, Dodo,” Celia continued, noticing only that Dorothea was leaning back in her chair and looked unlikely to resist, “is that Mr. Casaubon was spiteful. I never liked him, nor did James. The corners of his mouth always looked dreadfully spiteful to me. And now he’s behaved like this, I’m sure religion doesn’t require you to make yourself miserable over him. If he’s been taken away, it’s a mercy, and you ought to be grateful. We shouldn’t grieve, should we, baby?” Celia confided this to the unconscious center and balancing point of the world. His fists were extraordinary, complete down to the fingernails; and when his cap came off, he really had enough hair to make—you couldn’t say what. In short, he was a Western incarnation of Buddha.

At this critical moment Lydgate was announced. Almost his first words were, “I’m afraid you’re not as well as you were, Mrs. Casaubon. Has something upset you? May I feel your pulse?” Dorothea’s hand was as cold as marble.
“She wants to go to Lowick and examine papers,” said Celia. “She shouldn’t, should she?”

For a moment Lydgate said nothing. Then, looking at Dorothea, he answered, “I’m not quite sure. I think Mrs. Casaubon ought to do whatever will give her the greatest peace of mind. Preventing her from acting won’t always bring that peace.”

“Thank you,” said Dorothea, making an effort. “I’m sure you’re right. There are so many things I ought to attend to. Why should I sit here doing nothing?” Trying to summon up subjects unconnected with her distress, she added abruptly, “I think you know everyone in Middlemarch, Mr. Lydgate. I’ll have a great many questions for you. I have serious responsibilities now. I must appoint someone to a living. You know Mr. Tyke and all the—” But the effort was more than Dorothea could manage. She stopped and burst into tears.
Lydgate had her drink a dose of sal volatile, the restorative spirit.
Before leaving, he asked to speak to Sir James. “Let Mrs. Casaubon do what she wants,” he told him. “I think complete freedom is the treatment she needs most.”

Treating Dorothea during her mental agitation had allowed him to reach some accurate conclusions about the difficulties of her life. He was certain she had suffered from the strain and inner conflict of suppressing herself. Now she was likely to feel that she had merely exchanged one enclosure for another.

It became easier for Sir James to follow Lydgate’s advice when he discovered that Celia had already told Dorothea the unpleasant truth about the will. Nothing could be done about that now, and there was no reason to postpone necessary business any longer. The following day, when Dorothea asked him to drive her to Lowick, he agreed at once.

“I don’t want to stay there just yet,” Dorothea said. “I could hardly bear it. I’m much happier at Freshitt with Celia. Looking at Lowick from a distance will help me think more clearly about what should be done there. And I’d like to spend a little time with my uncle at the Grange, walking along all the old paths and visiting the people in the village.”

“Not yet, I think. Your uncle is entertaining political guests, and you’re better away from all that,” said Sir James, who was thinking of the Grange chiefly as a place young Ladislaw frequented. Neither he nor Dorothea mentioned the offensive clause in the will; both felt that speaking of it to each other would be impossible. Sir James was reluctant to discuss disagreeable matters even with other men. As for Dorothea, the one thing she would have chosen to say was something she could not bring herself to mention yet, because it would further expose her husband’s injustice. Still, she wished Sir James could know what she and her husband had said about Will Ladislaw’s moral claim to the property. Then, she thought, he would see as clearly as she did that her husband’s strange, indelicate condition sprang chiefly from his bitter resistance to that claim, and not simply from more intimate feelings that were harder to discuss. Admittedly, Dorothea also wanted this known for Will’s sake, since her friends seemed to regard him only as a recipient of Mr. Casaubon’s charity. Why compare him to an Italian carrying white mice? Those words of Mrs. Cadwallader’s seemed a mocking caricature sketched in darkness by a malicious imp.

At Lowick, Dorothea searched every desk and drawer, every place where her husband had kept private papers. She found nothing addressed specifically to her except the “Synoptical Tabulation,” probably the first of many intended instructions. In arranging this legacy of work for Dorothea, as in everything else, Mr. Casaubon had proceeded slowly and hesitantly. Planning how to pass on his work had oppressed him just as doing it had: he felt he was laboriously moving through something dark and obstructive. His doubts about Dorothea’s ability to arrange his materials were overcome only by his doubts about any other editor. Eventually, however, he had built himself a hope from Dorothea’s character. What she resolved to do, she could accomplish; and he readily pictured her laboring, bound by a promise, to build a tomb bearing his name. Not that Mr. Casaubon called the projected volumes a tomb: he called them the Key to all Mythologies. But the months overtook him and his plans fell behind. He had found time only to ask for the promise through which he hoped to maintain his cold grip on Dorothea’s life.

That grip had loosened. Had she bound herself by a promise made from the depths of pity, she could have undertaken work which her judgment quietly told her was useless—except as a sacred act of faithfulness, itself a supreme purpose. But now her judgment was no longer restrained by dutiful devotion. It had been stirred to action by the bitter discovery that secrecy and suspicion had concealed an estrangement within her marriage. The living, suffering man was no longer there to awaken her compassion. All that remained was the memory of painful submission to a husband whose thoughts had been less noble than she believed. His excessive demands on his own behalf had blinded even his meticulous concern for his reputation, defeating his own pride by shocking men with ordinary standards of honor. As for the property that represented their broken bond, she would gladly have surrendered it and kept only her own original fortune, secured to her at marriage, had ownership not brought duties she ought not to evade. Troubling questions about that property kept forcing themselves upon her. Hadn’t she been right to think half of it should go to Will Ladislaw? Yet wasn’t that act of justice now impossible? Mr. Casaubon had found a cruelly effective way to prevent it. Even while indignant with him, she recoiled from any action that looked like a triumphant circumvention of his wishes.

After gathering the business papers she wanted to study, she locked the desks and drawers again. They held no personal words for her, no sign that in her husband’s solitary brooding his heart had reached towards her with an explanation or apology. She returned to Freshitt feeling that his last harsh demand and final harmful assertion of power remained surrounded by unbroken silence.

Dorothea now tried to direct her thoughts to immediate duties. One of them was something other people were determined to remind her of. Lydgate had listened eagerly when she mentioned the living. At the first opportunity he returned to it, seeing a chance to make amends for the deciding vote he had once cast against his uneasy conscience. “Rather than tell you about Mr. Tyke,” he said, “I’d like to speak about another man—Mr. Farebrother, the Vicar of St. Botolph’s. His living brings in very little, barely enough to support him and his family. His mother, aunt and sister all live with him and depend on him. I believe they’re the reason he never married. I’ve never heard better preaching—such clear, natural eloquence. He could have followed old Latimer in the pulpit at St. Paul’s Cross. His conversation is equally good, whatever the subject: fresh, unpretentious and clear. I think he’s a remarkable man. He ought to have achieved more than he has.”
“Why hasn’t he?” asked Dorothea, whose interest now extended to everyone who had fallen short of their own intentions.

“That’s difficult to answer,” said Lydgate. “I’ve found myself that doing the right thing is extraordinarily hard: so many forces pull at you at once. Farebrother often suggests he chose the wrong profession. He needs a wider field than a poor clergyman has, and I suppose he lacks influential friends to help him advance. He’s very interested in natural history and various sciences, and struggles to fit those interests into his position. He has no money to spare—scarcely enough to live on—and that’s driven him to cards. Middlemarch is a great town for whist. He plays for money, certainly, and wins quite a lot. Naturally, that draws him into company somewhat beneath him and makes him careless about certain things. Yet taking him altogether, despite that, I think he’s one of the least blameworthy men I’ve known. There’s no malice or duplicity in him, and those qualities often accompany a more respectable exterior.”
“I wonder whether the habit troubles his conscience,” Dorothea said. “I wonder whether he wishes he could give it up.”
“I’m sure he’d abandon it if he had a comfortable income. He’d welcome the time for other interests.”

“My uncle says Mr. Tyke is described as an apostolic man,” Dorothea said thoughtfully. She wished the zeal of early Christianity could be restored, yet at the same time she felt a powerful desire to rescue Mr. Farebrother from earning money by games of chance.

“I wouldn’t claim Farebrother is apostolic,” said Lydgate. “His situation is rather different from the Apostles’. He’s simply a parson among parishioners whose lives he must try to improve. In practice, what people now call apostolic seems to mean impatience with anything in which the parson isn’t the leading figure. I see something of that in Mr. Tyke at the Hospital. Much of his teaching amounts to pinching people hard to make them uncomfortably aware of his presence. Besides, an apostolic man at Lowick! He’d have to decide, like St. Francis, that the birds needed preaching to.”

“That’s true,” said Dorothea. “It’s difficult to imagine what ideas our farmers and laborers get from the teaching they hear. I’ve been looking through a volume of Mr. Tyke’s sermons. Sermons like those would be useless at Lowick—I mean the ones about imputed righteousness and the prophecies of the Apocalypse. I’ve always thought about the different ways Christianity is taught. Whenever I find a way that makes it a greater blessing than any other, I hold to that as the truest. I mean the teaching that embraces the most goodness of every kind, and allows the most people to share in it. Surely it’s better to forgive too much than condemn too much. But I’d like to meet Mr. Farebrother and hear him preach.”

“Please do,” said Lydgate. “I’m confident that will persuade you. He’s greatly loved, though he has enemies too. There are always people who can’t forgive a capable man for disagreeing with them. And winning money at cards really is a blemish. Of course, you don’t see many Middlemarch people, but Mr. Ladislaw, who sees Mr. Brooke constantly, is a close friend of Mr. Farebrother’s old ladies. He’d gladly sing the Vicar’s praises. One of them—his aunt, Miss Noble—is a wonderfully quaint picture of goodness that never thinks of itself. Ladislaw sometimes escorts her about. I met them in a back street one day. You know how Ladislaw looks—a sort of Daphnis in a coat and waistcoat. With that little old maid reaching up to his arm, they looked like a pair who’d stepped out of a romantic comedy. Still, the best evidence about Farebrother is to meet him and hear him.”

Fortunately this conversation took place in Dorothea’s private sitting room. Nobody else was there to make Lydgate’s innocent mention of Ladislaw painful to her. As usually happened with personal gossip, Lydgate had entirely forgotten Rosamond’s remark that she thought Will adored Mrs. Casaubon. Just then he cared only about recommending the Farebrother family. He had deliberately emphasized the worst things that could be said about the Vicar in order to anticipate objections. He had scarcely seen Ladislaw in the weeks since Mr. Casaubon’s death, and no rumor had warned him that mentioning Mr. Brooke’s confidential secretary to Mrs. Casaubon might be dangerous. After he left, his picture of Ladislaw lingered in Dorothea’s mind, competing with the question of the Lowick living. What was Will Ladislaw thinking of her? Would he hear the fact that made her cheeks burn as they never had before? How would he feel when he knew? Yet she could picture perfectly his smile as he looked down at the little old maid. An Italian with white mice! On the contrary, he was someone who could enter into anyone’s feelings, accepting the pressure of their thoughts instead of forcing his own upon them with iron resistance.
